task.goal: Help a household share one bicycle without last-minute conflicts.
hard_constraints: Three adults use one bike and a paper calendar; no tracking app.
Keep personal trip destinations private and allow emergency use.
Compare missed trips, idle time and coordination effort for two weeks.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Reserve only the time you need
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the paper calendar as the sole booking record. Each adult writes an initial and departure–return window as soon as a trip becomes likely; destinations and purposes stay private. The first entry holds the bike. Overlapping requests require an agreed swap before either person relies on the bike. Release cancelled bookings promptly, and keep the key in one agreed place whenever the bike is home. Allow a realistic return buffer.

This changes the outcome by exposing conflicts early while leaving unbooked hours available to everyone. It requires people to check the calendar and return on time; uncertain schedules and habitual early booking could undermine it. No materials beyond the calendar, a writing implement and existing key are needed.

An emergency overrides an ordinary booking when the bike is home: tell the affected adult if reachable, mark an estimated return, and disclose no destination. A bike already away cannot be recalled reliably with these resources.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare seven days of the current routine with seven days of reservations, matching weekdays. On the calendar, tally intended trips missed because the bike was unavailable, approximate daylight hours the bike sat unused, and minutes spent checking, discussing or recording arrangements. Include measurement effort consistently in both weeks. Also mark booked windows that went unused. The mechanism is doubtful if missed trips do not fall, or if unused reservations and coordination effort rise substantially. Two weeks provide a preliminary comparison; different trip demand or emergencies could explain differences.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Rotate predictable priority periods
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Divide each day into morning, afternoon and evening periods on the calendar. Assign priority to the three adults in a repeating rotation, shifting the starting adult each day. The priority adult marks whether they need their period by the preceding evening; otherwise it becomes open. Another adult may reserve a released period by initialling it. Trips must finish before the next claimed period, including a return buffer. Keep the key in a fixed place when the bike is home.

Predictable ownership reduces repeated negotiation and distributes desirable periods across people. Only initials and times appear, keeping destinations private. Implementation needs one initial calendar setup and brief daily checks. It assumes most trips fit the periods and that adults can sometimes shift departure times. Long or inflexible trips require an explicit swap, and unequal demand may make equal priority inefficient.

Emergency use takes precedence whenever the bike is present, with notice to the displaced adult where possible and an estimated return on the calendar. It cannot guarantee access while someone is riding.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use the current routine for week one and rotating priority for week two. Record daily missed intended trips caused by bike availability, approximate unused daylight hours, and coordination minutes. Mark whether each missed trip fell inside someone else's claimed but unused period. Before starting, agree what increase in effort or idle time would outweigh fewer missed trips. Reject or revise the routine if rigid periods themselves cause repeated misses or claimed periods sit empty. Compare matching weekdays, while noting that a single week per condition cannot establish a reliable causal effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Allocate conflicts by fewest recent rides
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Each evening, adults enter only their next day's desired departure–return windows and initials on the calendar. Nonoverlapping requests stand automatically. For an overlap, priority goes to whoever has completed the fewest bike trips during the preceding seven days, counted from small completion ticks on the calendar. Break ties using a rotating initial order written at the top. Resolve conflicts that evening; later requests fit around confirmed windows unless everyone affected agrees to change them. Cancel unused requests promptly and return the key to its agreed place.

The mechanism gives a clear, inspectable answer to competing requests while compensating people who have used the shared bike less. It needs a short evening check and one tick per completed outing, without recording destinations. It assumes ride counts are an acceptable fairness measure: a short outing and a long outing count equally, so this may fit poorly where needs differ sharply. It also exposes usage frequency, although personal destinations remain private.

An emergency overrides the allocation when the bike is home, without requiring disclosure of its purpose. Notify displaced users if possible and mark the expected return. Emergency rides also receive completion ticks.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare one week of the current routine with one week using the rule. Tally bike-related missed intended trips, approximate unused daylight hours and coordination minutes on the calendar. Inspect each contested window: was the decision settled the evening before, and did the winner actually use it? The rule fails its basic purpose if conflicts still require last-minute bargaining, or if fewer rides merely redistribute missed trips without an acceptable fairness benefit. Ask each adult privately whether the allocation felt workable; two weeks cannot establish longer-term fairness.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Fit flexible trips around fixed ones
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a brief evening scheduling check to fit the next day's trips together. Each adult writes only initials, expected bike-use duration including a return buffer, and earliest departure/latest return. Someone with a fixed appointment can give a narrow window without explaining why. No destinations or purposes are recorded.

Together, place the least flexible trips first, then fit flexible trips into the remaining gaps. Confirm actual departure–return times on the calendar before ending the check. Entry order gives no priority. If two trips cannot both fit, ask whether either person can shift; if neither can, use a rotating tie-break initial and acknowledge the unresolved missed trip in advance. Late requests use remaining gaps or require agreement from affected adults.

The working principle is to use scheduling flexibility to preserve trips that would otherwise collide. This differs from awarding an overlap to the first claimant: a flexible request can move so both people ride. It assumes adults know roughly how long they need and that some trips can shift. If everyone's timing is fixed, this routine offers little benefit and may add discussion.

Implementation needs the existing calendar, key, an available pen, and a short shared check. Keep the key in one agreed place when home and cross out cancelled allocations. An emergency may override the schedule whenever the bike is present, without disclosing its destination or purpose; mark an expected return and notify displaced users if reachable. Access cannot be guaranteed while someone is riding.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
For seven days, retain the current routine; for the next seven, use flexible-window scheduling. In both weeks, tally daily intended trips missed because the bike was unavailable, approximate hours the bike was home and unused within the same agreed daily observation period, and total person-minutes spent coordinating and recording measurements. Compare matching weekdays and note total requested trips.

During the trial week, mark each occasion when shifting a flexible trip allowed both requests to happen. Inspect after three days: if no requests can shift and discussion takes longer, the proposed mechanism has little support. After two weeks, judge whether fewer misses justify any added effort or idle time. This is a preliminary comparison; changing demand and emergencies can explain differences.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Use a waiting queue with bounded loans
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use the calendar as a same-day waiting queue rather than allocating future time slots. An adult who wants the bike writes their initial and latest useful departure time, without a destination or purpose. Cross out requests that expire or are withdrawn. When the bike returns, the earliest still-active entry gets the next turn; skip anyone who is not ready to leave. With no waiting entries, anyone may take it.

Agree on a normal maximum loan length that accommodates common local trips. Before leaving, the borrower checks the queue and writes an expected return. If someone is waiting, the borrower must return within that limit. A longer outing requires agreement from those already waiting. Return the key to one agreed place and tell the next waiting adult that the bike is back when practical.

The mechanism is a work-conserving queue: the bike keeps moving between ready users, while bounded loans stop one discretionary outing from blocking several others. It could suit a household whose trips are mostly short and whose departure times tolerate some waiting. It assumes adults can check the calendar, communicate at home, and honor return estimates. Fixed appointments, long essential trips, and requests entered while the bike is already away remain weaknesses. Implementation needs only calendar space, an existing writing implement, the key, and a brief agreement on the loan limit.

An emergency goes ahead of the queue whenever the bike is home. Mark an expected return and notify displaced adults if reachable; no explanation or destination is required. Emergency access cannot be guaranteed while the bike is away.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Keep the current routine for seven days, then try the queue for seven. In both weeks, tally bike-related missed intended trips, approximate home-and-unused hours during the same daily observation period, and total person-minutes spent coordinating and recording. Count trips abandoned because the loan limit was too short as missed trips. Compare matching weekdays and note demand and emergencies. Inspect the first three contested returns: did the next ready adult actually get the bike promptly? Repeated empty handoffs, excessive checking, or more missed trips would undermine the mechanism. The two-week comparison is preliminary because demand may differ.

EXPAND.title: Fit flexible requests together before fixing departure times
EXPAND.proposal:
Allocate the next day's bike use by fitting trips into acceptable time ranges. Each adult writes an initial, earliest acceptable departure, latest acceptable return and required bike duration, including a return buffer. No destination or purpose is recorded. An adult designated as that evening's coordinator proposes exact departure–return slots that accommodate the most requests. Each affected adult confirms their slot before relying on it. Rotate coordinator duty daily.

For three requests, try the six possible rider orders on paper. If all three cannot fit, use a rotating tie-break order to choose between equally successful schedules; explicitly mark unallocated requests that evening. Late requests use remaining gaps. Cancellations release their slots, but nobody's confirmed time moves without agreement. Return the key to one agreed place whenever the bike comes home.

The mechanism uses flexibility that first-entry reservations can waste: an early flexible request can move so a later inflexible request also fits. It assumes adults can specify truthful acceptable ranges and sometimes adjust departure times. Maximizing trip count can disadvantage long trips, so this needs household acceptance and may prove unsuitable. It requires only the calendar, its usual writing implement, the key and a brief evening check.

An adult declaring an emergency may take the bike when it is home, informing displaced users if reachable and writing an estimated return without disclosing a destination. Access cannot be guaranteed while the bike is away.
EXPAND.experiment: Run first-entry reservations for seven days, then flexible scheduling for seven days, comparing matching weekdays. A designated tally owner records daily bike-related missed trips, approximate idle hours within the same agreed observation window, and total coordination minutes, including measurement. Mark whether moving a flexible request actually saved another trip and whether long trips were displaced. Stop the challenger early if anyone repeatedly receives times outside their stated limits. Keep it only if its reduction in missed trips justifies the added scheduling effort without unacceptable displacement of long trips. If requests rarely have usable flexibility, expect no improvement over simple reservations. Two weeks give preliminary evidence; demand differences remain a confounder.

EXPAND.title: Limit checkout length when several people need the bike
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a short checkout limit to stop one long outing consuming the shared bike's usable day. Before the trial, all three adults agree on a maximum ordinary checkout duration that covers common short trips, including a return buffer. On the calendar, record next-day requests as initials and ready-to-leave times. Requests enter a queue in order of readiness; rotate priority for ties. The first ready adult takes the bike and writes the return deadline. On return, put the key in its agreed place and notify the next queued adult directly when reachable.

A queued adult who cannot leave when offered the bike yields to the next ready person and rejoins when ready. Nobody should rely on an exact departure until the preceding rider returns. An outing exceeding the limit is allowed only if every other adult explicitly releases their competing claim for that interval; otherwise it cannot use this routine. Nobody must disclose why or where they are going.

The outcome-changing mechanism is limiting how long a rider can block others, rather than deciding who wins an overlapping reservation. It may serve several short trips during a period otherwise occupied by one long checkout. It assumes typical trips fit the limit and riders can tolerate uncertain starts. It can shift harm onto long trips and create waiting, so it is unsuitable for many fixed appointments. Resources are the existing calendar, writing implement and key.

Emergency use overrides the queue whenever the bike is home, without a destination disclosure. Notify waiting adults if possible and record an estimated return. Emergencies cannot recall a bike already away.
EXPAND.experiment: A rotating daily queue steward manages a seven-day trial after seven days of first-entry reservations. In both weeks, tally missed intended trips caused by bike access, approximate idle hours over identical observation windows and coordination minutes. Also record waiting minutes and trips excluded solely by the checkout limit. Compare matching weekdays. Stop early if an agreed essential trip is prevented by the limit or repeated handoffs fail. Reject the routine if extra completed short trips are offset by excluded long trips, excessive waiting or more coordination than the household accepts. The two-week comparison is exploratory, particularly if trip lengths differ between weeks.

EXPAND.title: P0 improvement: reservations with explicit release and late-return recovery
EXPAND.proposal:
Keep P0’s first-entry reservations, adding a rule that prevents someone relying on a bike that has not returned. Write only initials and departure–return windows, including a realistic buffer. Resolve overlaps before confirming a trip; return the key to one agreed place whenever the bike is home. Cancelled windows become available immediately.

At departure, a reservation authorizes use only if the bike and key are present. If the preceding rider is late, mark the affected request as delayed; do not silently shift later reservations. A delayed rider may use a remaining gap only if they can return before the next booking, or obtain that adult’s agreement. If neither works, release the request and count it as missed. Anyone anticipating lateness tells affected adults directly when feasible; this cannot depend on having a phone. Emergency use overrides ordinary bookings whenever the bike is home: give notice if reachable and enter an estimated return, without recording a destination or reason.

The specific fix is an availability gate plus bounded recovery, preserving P0’s simple booking mechanism. It assumes adults check the calendar and give credible return estimates; it cannot recover a bike already away. Resources are the calendar, its usual writing implement and existing key.

Compared with P1’s rotating periods, P0 better accommodates irregular journeys but permits early bookers to dominate. P1 reduces negotiation but can strand usable time or require swaps. Ride-count priority adds accounting without addressing lateness; flexible scheduling adds evening coordination; checkout limits shift costs onto long trips. This revision targets cascading delays, although missed trips may merely become more explicit.
EXPAND.experiment: One adult maintains the totals for 14 days. Use ordinary P0 for week one and this revision for week two, comparing matched weekdays where possible. Each adult records destination-free counts of requests missed because of bike access and coordination minutes; record actual checkout–return times to calculate bike-at-home minutes during one agreed daily observation window. Separately tally delayed departures to detect displaced waiting costs. Stop the revision if recovery repeatedly requires lengthy negotiations; revert to ordinary P0 with explicit agreement for each disrupted booking. No gain is demonstrated if missed trips stay unchanged while coordination or waiting increases. Weekly demand differences limit interpretation.

EXPAND.title: Departure clearance: resolve competing needs before taking the key
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a brief departure clearance instead of advance reservations. Before an ordinary checkout, the rider proposes a return deadline directly to both other adults. Each answers either “clear” or gives the latest time they need the bike, without describing any destination. Departure requires both adults’ clearance for the proposed interval. Put only the rider’s initial and promised return on the calendar; the key leaves with the rider and returns to its fixed place.

This changes the outcome through explicit acknowledgement: an unrecorded imminent need can stop a departure before the bike disappears. If needs overlap, first try a shorter checkout that both accept. Otherwise, use a rotating initial order on the calendar to decide who receives the contested interval, provided that rider has confirmed that the interval works. The others record any resulting missed request. Once cleared, that interval stands; new ordinary requests wait until the bike returns. A rider expecting lateness informs affected adults when feasible; on return, confirm availability directly if someone is waiting.

Emergency use takes precedence whenever the bike is present, without requiring clearance or disclosure of its purpose. Mark an estimated return and notify affected adults if reachable. Emergency access remains impossible while the bike is away.

This needs only the existing calendar, writing implement and key, but assumes the three adults are commonly reachable in person. Silence is not clearance. If either adult cannot be reached, ordinary departure waits; if this blocks a needed trip, end the clearance routine and use calendar reservations for subsequent trips: initials, agreed departure–return windows, first entry holds, overlapping requests require an agreed swap. This fallback makes availability practical without treating absence as consent. Clearance may prevent surprise conflicts, but can shift substantial costs into interruptions and delayed departures.
EXPAND.experiment: One adult totals a bounded 14-day comparison: calendar reservations in week one, departure clearance in week two. Record missed requests, actual checkout–return times for bike-at-home minutes within the same daily observation window, and each adult’s coordination minutes. Also tally departures delayed solely by waiting for replies. Stop clearance immediately if an unreachable adult blocks a needed ordinary trip, and use the stated reservation fallback for the remaining days; retain that failure in the results. Clearance fails its practical test if it prevents no additional missed trips or its interruptions and waiting outweigh any improvement. Differences in weekly demand remain uncertain.
